title: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis
question_text:
What is the characteristic sign on non-contrast CT?
What is the definitive treatment in case of non- functioning kidney?
correct_answer:
1) Bear-paw sign
2) Nephrectomy | Bear-paw sign, Nephrectomy | Bear paw sign and nephrectomy | Bear-paw sign | Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis | XGP
explanation:
CT shows an enlarged left kidney with a large calculus (possibly staghorn) at the renal pelvis with dilated calyces with hypodense content within, which represents xanthogranulomatous content.
In the setting of a diabetic patient with recurrent UTIs, xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis becomes the primary differential.
In acute hydronephrosis, the content within the calyces are fluid attenuating.
Xanthogranulomatous content is usually denser.
key_findings:
Obstructive calculus
Dilated renal calyces with hypodense content
learning_points:
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a chronic suppurative renal infection, classically unilateral, in middle-aged women with obstructing calculi (often staghorn) and recurrent infection, and it is more frequent in diabetic patients.
On CT the enlarged kidney shows multiple dilated calyces filled with low-attenuation xanthomatous material (denser than simple hydronephrotic fluid) surrounding a central calculus, giving the "bear paw" sign. The kidney is usually non-functioning, and the inflammation may extend into the perirenal and pararenal spaces.
Treatment is antibiotics followed by nephrectomy when the kidney is non-functioning.
differential_diagnosis: Obstructive hydronephrosis

title: Sarcoidosis
clinical_info: 40 year- old woman with dry cough
question_text:
What is the name of the sign?
Elucidate the characteristic histopathological finding.
correct_answer:
1) Garland triad
2) Non-caseating granulomas | Garland triad, Non-caseating granulomas | Garland triad | Garland sign | 1-2-3 sign | Sarcoidosis
explanation:
Plain radiograph of the chest shows enlarged and lobulated bilateral hila (compare the the hilar thickness to the right/ left bronchial lumen diameter).
The right paratracheal stripe is also widened.
These three features denote the classical Garland sign, where there are enlarged lymph nodes in the right paratracheal region and bilateral hilar regions.
key_findings: Hilar and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy
learning_points: When both the hila are enlarged, check if they are smooth or lobulated. Smooth hilar enlargement favours pulmonary arterial dilation and hence pulmonary hypertension. Lobulated hilar contour usually denotes lymphadenopathy.
differential_diagnosis: Other causes of mediastinal lymphadenopathy such as lymphoma, granulomatous or metastatic disease

title: Eagle Syndrome
question_text:
What structure(s) are abnormal?
What is the length of the structure above which is considered abnormal?
correct_answer:
1) Elongated styloid process or calcified stylohyoid ligament
2) Abnormal when > 3 cm | Elongated styloid process, > 3 cm | Elongated styloid process | Calcified stylohyoid ligament | Eagle syndrome
explanation: Plain radiograph of the neck, lateral view shows an elongated styloid process.
key_findings: Elongated styloid process
learning_points: Always evaluate styloid process on neck radiographs and CTs for this entity

title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage
question_text:
What is the most common non-traumatic cause of this appearance, and which artery is most frequently implicated?
What follow-up imaging identifies the underlying vascular cause?
correct_answer:
1) Ruptured saccular aneurysm is the most common cause; the anterior communicating artery is the single most common site.
2) CT angiography is first-line to localise and characterise the aneurysm; catheter DSA remains the gold standard if CTA is negative but suspicion persists. | Ruptured saccular aneurysm, Anterior communicating artery, CT angiography | Ruptured berry aneurysm, ACom, CTA | Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage | Subarachnoid hemorrhage | Ruptured saccular aneurysm
explanation:
Non-contrast CT of the head shows hyperdense (acute) blood filling the basal cisterns and sylvian fissures, outlining the suprasellar and perimesencephalic cisterns.
A sudden, severe (thunderclap) headache is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Non-contrast CT performed within the first 6 hours is almost 100% sensitive when read by an experienced radiologist, and sensitivity falls steadily over the following days as blood is cleared.
The commonest non-traumatic cause is rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm at the circle of Willis.
key_findings:
Hyperdensity within the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures and interhemispheric fissure
Blood may extend into the ventricles (intraventricular haemorrhage) or the brain parenchyma
Hydrocephalus (dilated temporal horns) from obstruction of CSF absorption
Aneurysm sites: anterior communicating artery (most common), posterior communicating artery, middle cerebral artery bifurcation, basilar tip
learning_points:
The distribution of blood gives a clue to the source. Blood in the anterior interhemispheric fissure suggests an anterior communicating artery aneurysm, blood in the sylvian fissure suggests a middle cerebral artery aneurysm, and blood in the posterior fossa suggests a posterior circulation aneurysm.
Complications to look for are re-bleeding (highest in the first 24 hours), delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (typically days 4 to 14), and acute hydrocephalus. The modified Fisher scale grades the amount of blood and predicts vasospasm risk.
If CTA is negative and clinical suspicion persists, digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is performed, sometimes repeated after 1 to 2 weeks.
differential_diagnosis:
Traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage: convexity location, with adjacent contusions or fractures
Perimesencephalic (non-aneurysmal) subarachnoid haemorrhage: blood confined anterior to the midbrain/pons, with a benign course
Arteriovenous malformation or dural arteriovenous fistula
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome: convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage with thunderclap headache
Pseudo-subarachnoid haemorrhage: diffuse cerebral oedema or hypoxic injury makes the cisterns look dense

title: Pheochromocytoma
question_text:
What is the classic T2-weighted MRI appearance of this lesion called?
Name the other components of MEN 2B syndrome.
correct_answer:
1) Light-bulb sign
2) Medullary thyroid carcinoma, Mucosal neuromas, Marfanoid habitus | Light-bulb sign, Medullary thyroid carcinoma, Mucosal neuromas, Marfanoid habitus | Light bulb sign | Pheochromocytoma | Phaeochromocytoma
explanation:
On T2, these lesions appear very hyperintense, and hence, appear as a ‘Light bulb’
MEN 2B syndrome is characterized by phaeochromocytoma, Medullary thyroid carcinoma, Mucosal neuromas, Marfanoid habitus
key_findings: CECT abdomen shows avidly, but heterogeneously enhancing lesion anterior to the left kidney.
learning_points:
In a patient with hypertension and avidly enhancing lesion along the sympathetic chain, consideration of phaeochromocytoma is primary.
They show intense arterial phase enhancement, with attenuation values more than 120 HU and are usually heterogeneous.
When arising from extra- adrenal sites, they are termed as ‘Paragangliomas’
differential_diagnosis: Carcinoid tumors (usually arises from the mesentery/ pancreas/ small bowel)

title: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)
question_text:
What is the procedure done here and what is the physiological rationale for this procedure?
What shunt velocity value raises concern for stenosis?
correct_answer:
1) Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) creation. TIPS creates a low-resistance portal-to-hepatic venous channel, reducing portal pressure and thereby flow through varices and ascites formation.
2) Shunt velocity < 90 cm/s or > 190 cm/s | TIPS, < 90 cm/s or > 190 cm/s | Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt | TIPS
explanation:
Colour Doppler ultrasound shows an echogenic stent traversing the liver parenchyma between the portal vein and a hepatic vein, with colour filling of the lumen.
TIPS decompresses the portal circulation by diverting portal blood directly into the hepatic venous system (and then the inferior vena cava), bypassing the cirrhotic sinusoidal resistance. It is used mainly for refractory ascites and for variceal bleeding that fails endoscopic and medical therapy.
Doppler surveillance looks for shunt dysfunction. Peak velocities within the stent are normally about 90 to 190 cm/s. Values outside this range, or a fall of more than about 50 cm/s from baseline, suggest stenosis or thrombosis.
key_findings:
Echogenic stent walls seen as parallel bright lines through the liver
Colour fill of the entire stent lumen, with turbulent but forward flow
Peak intrastent velocity within the 90 to 190 cm/s range when functioning
Dysfunction: low velocity, absent flow, focal velocity jump, or return of ascites and varices
learning_points:
The commonest site of stenosis is the hepatic venous end of the stent (from pseudo-intimal hyperplasia), followed by the parenchymal tract. Covered stent-grafts have much better patency than bare stents.
Important complication: hepatic encephalopathy, because portal blood bypasses the liver.
Doppler is the first-line surveillance tool, and a suspicious study is followed by venography and pressure gradient measurement with possible revision.
differential_diagnosis:
Shunt stenosis (hepatic vein end or intrastent)
Shunt thrombosis or occlusion
Stent migration or malposition
Hepatic vein outflow obstruction or Budd-Chiari physiology (the indication for TIPS in some patients)

title: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA)
question_text:
What pathognomonic sign is seen and what does it indicate?
What procedure is recommended before surgical resection?
correct_answer:
1) Holman-Miller sign: anterior bowing/erosion of the posterior maxillary sinus wall, reflecting origin at the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa.
2) Catheter angiography with pre-operative embolization precedes surgical resection. | Holman-Miller sign, Pre-operative embolization | Holman-Miller sign | Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma | JNA
explanation: On CECT, there is a mass centred in the right pterygopalatine fossa, insinuating into the connected spaces, anteriorly causing bowing of the posterior maxillary sinus wall, medially into the nasopharynx/ nasal cavity, laterally into the pterygomaxillary fissure. These lesions show avid enhancement which reflects their high vascularity. Hence, pre- operative embolization reduces surgical risk of bleeding.
key_findings: CECT shows avidly, but heterogeneously enhancing lesion centered in the sphenopalatine foramen/ pterygopalatine fossa with anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus (Holman- Miller sign)
learning_points: In a young patient with epistaxis and avidly enhancing lesion centred at the sphenopalatine foramen/ pterygopalatine fossa, think of JNA
differential_diagnosis:
Rhabdomyosarcoma- usually more invasive. Typically, has low ADC values
Esthesioneuroblastoma- centred in the nasal cavity roof with cysts at the superior margin.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma- lacks prominent flow voids on MRI and is more invasive

title: CNS lymphoma
clinical_info: 68 year old man with altered sensorium
question_text:
What characteristic imaging features differentiate this lesion from a high grade astrocytoma?
What is the rationale of withholding steroids initially in this case?
correct_answer:
1) Lymphoma shows relatively homogeneous restricted diffusion and enhancement compared to GBM. It has a lower RCBV on perfusion studies
2) Steroids rapidly shrink the tumor and can cause the visible enhancing mass on an MRI to completely disappear within days. Because lymphoma cells die off quickly, pathologists may only see dying cells or reactive tissue, making it impossible to identify the specific type of lymphoma | Homogeneous restricted diffusion and enhancement, low rCBV, steroids cause rapid tumor lysis/vanishing tumor | Primary CNS lymphoma | CNS lymphoma
explanation:
On MRI, a periventricular lesion which is relatively homogeneous, with restricted diffusion and relatively uniform enhancement, small round cell tumours become the primary differential.
Due to densely packed cells, these tumors show restricted diffusion and lack of necrosis would mean they enhance homogeneously compared to GBM. RCBV is lower than GBM due to denser architecture of cells.
key_findings: DWI shows relatively homogeneous high signal in the periventricular region, in the splenium of the corpus callosum with corresponding low ADC values. There is homogeneous enhancement on post- contrast study.
learning_points: A large mass with relatively homogeneous characteristics, with restricted diffusion and contrast enhancement would usually point towards a small round cell tumour, such as lymphoma.
differential_diagnosis:
Secondary CNS lymphoma: tends to involve more leptomeninges
Cerebral toxoplasmosis- multifocal lesions in the basal ganglia, more so showing peripheral enhancement. Have higher RCBV
Butterfly glioma/GBM-  heterogeneous
Tumefactive MS/ ADEM

title: Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)
question_text:
What is the pattern called and likely cause in this case?
What are its four required Fleischner Society diagnostic features?
correct_answer:
1) Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern; Scleroderma (in view of dilated esophagus)
2) Definite UIP requires: - Subpleural/ basal predominance- Reticular pattern- Honeycombing (+/- traction bronchiectasis)- Absence of features suggesting an alternative diagnosis. | Usual interstitial pneumonia, Scleroderma | UIP pattern, Scleroderma | Usual interstitial pneumonia | UIP
explanation: On CT, there is honeycombing with bronchiolectasis and reticulation. The esophagus appears dilated.
key_findings: Honeycombing i.e clustered cystic airspaces—typically measuring 3 to 10 mm in diameter (though occasionally up to 2.5 cm)—with well-defined, thick walls (1–3 mm) that indicate established, irreversible pulmonary fibrosis.
learning_points:
Honeycombing is the hallmark of definite UIP.
Look for other clues for the cause, such as a dilated esophagus in scleroderma.
differential_diagnosis:
Paraseptal emphysema
Smoking-related interstitial fibrosis
Paracicatricial emphysema

title: Double duct sign
question_text:
What is the cause of this sign?
What vessel characteristics denote involvement by PDAC as per NCCN?
correct_answer:
1) Periampullary lesions that involve/ obstruct the distal common bile duct and main pancreatic duct
2) Vessel wall irregularity, tear drop sign, thrombosis, vessel encasement (> 180 degrees) | Periampullary lesion, Double duct sign | Periampullary carcinoma | Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma | Double duct sign
explanation:
On MRCP, there is dilation of both the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct. This is usually seen in mass lesions in the periampullary region.
In pre- surgical planning, what is considered vessel involvement, depends on the classification and if the vessel is an artery or a vein. Common classifications used are: NCCN and DPCG
key_findings: Dilated common bile duct and main pancreatic duct
learning_points:
Dilated common bile duct and main pancreatic duct together raise suspicion of a periampullary lesion.
A double duct sign should be treated as malignant until proven otherwise, since roughly half or more of cases in older series were malignant. Many resectable tumors are found at this stage.
differential_diagnosis:
Neoplastic (most important to exclude)- PDAC, ampullary carcinoma/adenoma, distal CBD cholangiocarcinoma, duodenal (periampullary) carcinoma
Neuroendocrine tumor
IPMN
Pancreatitis
Impacted ampullary or distal CBD stone
Papillary stenosis / sphincter of Oddi dysfunction

title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
question_text:
What finding indicates dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction?
What does mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement signify, and why is it prognostically important?
correct_answer:
1) Systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve toward the hypertrophied septum, with a turbulent LVOT jet on color Doppler, indicates dynamic obstruction.
2) Mid-wall (non-coronary distribution) LGE reflects fibrosis and is an independent risk factor for ventricular arrhythmia/ sudden death. | Systolic anterior motion (SAM) of mitral valve, Mid-wall LGE fibrosis | SAM of mitral valve | Systolic anterior motion | Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy | HCM | HOCM
explanation:
In HCM, a hypertrophied basal septum narrows the LVOT. During systole, the high-velocity flow through this narrowed channel creates a Venturi effect (drag and suction forces) that pulls the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum. This systolic anterior motion (SAM) produces septal contact, worsens the obstruction and causes posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation. The gradient is “dynamic” because it varies with preload, afterload and contractility (worse with Valsalva, dehydration, exercise or inotropes).
LGE reflects expansion of the extracellular space (gadolinium retention in myocardial fibrosis or scar). In HCM, it classically appears as patchy, mid-wall enhancement in hypertrophied segments, particularly at the right ventricular insertion points. It arises from myocyte disarray, small-vessel disease and replacement fibrosis, and it creates a substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias. This explains why LGE is an independent predictor of sudden cardiac death and arrhythmia, with risk increasing with extent (commonly cited threshold ≥15% of LV mass).
key_findings:
SAM of the anterior mitral leaflet (or chordae) on cine SSFP in the LVOT view
Signal void (flow-related dephasing) in the LVOT extending into the aortic root during systole
Posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation jet
Asymmetric basal septal hypertrophy (septal thickness ≥15 mm; ratio to the inferolateral wall >1.5)
Patchy mid-wall LGE in hypertrophied segments, non-coronary distribution (sparing the subendocardium)
Frequent enhancement at the anterior and inferior RV insertion points
learning_points:
Dynamic obstruction is a continuous variable, so provocation (Valsalva) may be needed to unmask it.
Planning LVOT views and SSFP cine is essential. Look for the mid-to-late systolic timing, which distinguishes it from fixed obstruction.
Identifying obstruction and its mechanism guides therapy (beta-blockers, septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation).
Mid-wall LGE is a pattern of non-ischemic fibrosis, and its extent adds risk-stratification value beyond conventional risk factors (family history, syncope, maximal wall thickness, non-sustained VT).
Extensive LGE helps decide on ICD placement in patients at borderline risk.
differential_diagnosis:
Dilated cardiomyopathy: linear mid-wall (septal) stripe in a dilated, hypokinetic ventricle, also carrying arrhythmic risk. The ventricular morphology differs from HCM.
Myocarditis: subepicardial or mid-wall LGE, often in the inferolateral wall, with accompanying edema (T2 or T1 mapping) in the acute phase.
Cardiac sarcoidosis: patchy mid-wall or subepicardial LGE, often basal septum or inferolateral wall, with possible nodal and extracardiac disease.
Fabry disease: basal inferolateral mid-wall LGE with low native T1 and concentric hypertrophy.
Cardiac amyloidosis: diffuse subendocardial or transmural LGE with high native T1 and ECV, and abnormal nulling of the myocardium.

title: Acquired cholesteatoma (pars flaccida type)
question_text:
Which landmark is characteristically eroded first, and where does this lesion typically originate?
What MRI sequence best differentiates residual/recurrent disease from post-operative granulation tissue?
correct_answer:
1) Scutum erosion is an early, characteristic finding; pars flaccida cholesteatoma arises in Prussak's space (lateral epitympanic recess).
2) Non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI shows restricted diffusion in cholesteatoma, distinguishing it from granulation tissue/ fluid. | Scutum erosion, Prussak space, Non-EPI DWI | Scutum erosion, Non-echo-planar DWI | Acquired cholesteatoma | Pars flaccida cholesteatoma | Cholesteatoma
explanation:
Cholesteatoma is an expansile collection of keratinizing squamous epithelium and keratin debris within the middle ear and mastoid. The pars flaccida (acquired attic) type is the commonest. Retraction of the pars flaccida creates a pocket that extends into Prussak’s space (lateral epitympanic recess), bounded by the pars flaccida laterally, the malleus neck medially and the scutum superiorly-laterally. As keratin accumulates, the mass enlarges and presses on the adjacent scutum, the sharp bony spur of the lateral epitympanic wall. This is the first bony landmark to blunt or erode, which is why scutum erosion is the earliest and most characteristic CT sign.
After surgery, the challenge is separating residual or recurrent cholesteatoma from granulation tissue, fluid or scar, since all appear as soft tissue on CT and may enhance. Non-echo-planar (non-EPI) DWI (e.g., HASTE or turbo spin-echo based) exploits the keratin content of cholesteatoma, which shows restricted diffusion (high DWI signal, low ADC). Granulation tissue and fluid do not. Non-EPI techniques avoid the susceptibility artifacts at the skull base and air-bone interfaces that degrade EPI DWI, and they can detect lesions as small as 2 to 3 mm.
key_findings:
HRCT: non-dependent soft tissue in Prussak’s space, blunted or eroded scutum, medial displacement or erosion of the ossicles (lateral malleus/incus body), and an enlarged epitympanum or aditus.
Non-EPI DWI: marked hyperintensity with low ADC.
Complications: erosion of the tegmen, lateral semicircular canal fistula, facial nerve canal dehiscence, sigmoid plate erosion.
learning_points:
Scutum blunting is the earliest sign, and the soft tissue in the attic with a normal-looking ossicular chain does not exclude disease.
Use non-EPI DWI with delayed post-contrast T1 for follow-up. This often avoids unnecessary “second-look” surgery.
Small lesions (<3 mm) and those with bright T1 or susceptibility from surgical material can give false negatives or positives.
differential_diagnosis:
Granulation tissue/chronic otitis media: T2 hyperintense with avid enhancement and no restricted diffusion.
Cholesterol granuloma: T1 and T2 hyperintense, with no restricted diffusion and no enhancement, and a bluish drum on otoscopy.
Middle ear fluid or mucosal thickening: no restricted diffusion, with a dependent distribution.
Congenital cholesteatoma: a retrotympanic mass behind an intact drum in a child, without a history of perforation.
Glomus tympanicum or schwannoma: an enhancing mass, with glomus tympanicum showing “salt-and-pepper” appearance and a promontorial location.

title: Tetralogy of Fallot
clinical_info: 6-month-old infant with an systolic ejection murmur.
question_text:
What four anatomic components constitute this condition?
Which component determines clinical severity?
correct_answer:
1) Ventricular septal defect, Overriding aorta, RVOT (subpulmonic) obstruction, RV hypertrophy.
2) Degree of RVOT obstruction determines severity of cyanosis. | VSD, Overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RV hypertrophy; RVOT obstruction | Tetralogy of Fallot | TOF | RVOT obstruction
explanation:
There is elevated left apex of the heart, giving rise to a boot- shaped heart or coeur en sabot
Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterior and cephalad displacement of the infundibular septum. This produces a malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta and narrowing of the RVOT, with RV hypertrophy developing secondarily from the pressure load.
The degree of RVOT obstruction determines severity: with mild obstruction, shunting is left-to-right (“pink tet”), while severe obstruction drives right-to-left shunting across the VSD and cyanosis.
key_findings:
VSD: large, subaortic, perimembranous malalignment type
Overriding aorta: aortic root straddles the septum (usually <50%)
RVOT obstruction: infundibular, valvar or supravalvar pulmonary stenosis, with hypoplastic pulmonary annulus or branch PAs
RV hypertrophy: thickened RV free wall
Associated: right aortic arch (~25%), coronary anomalies (e.g., LAD from RCA), ASD (pentalogy), MAPCAs
CXR: boot-shaped heart with oligaemic lungs
learning_points:
The infundibular septal malalignment is the primary defect, and the other components follow from it.
Pre-operative imaging should define coronary course, PA size and MAPCAs.
Post-repair MRI is used to quantify pulmonary regurgitation and RV volumes, which guide timing of valve replacement.
differential_diagnosis:
Double outlet right ventricle (Fallot type): more than 50% of the aorta arises from the RV.
Pulmonary atresia with VSD: no RV-to-PA continuity, with PA supply from MAPCAs or a PDA.
Transposition with VSD and pulmonary stenosis: discordant ventriculoarterial connections.
Eisenmenger syndrome: a large shunt with pulmonary hypertension, but no RVOT obstruction.

title: Multiple sclerosis
clinical_info: 29-year-old woman with recurrent episodes of optic neuritis.
question_text:
What are these periventricular lesions called, and what is their pathological basis?
What additional MRI feature distinguishes an active demyelinating plaque from a chronic lesion?
correct_answer:
1) "Dawson's fingers" reflect perivenular demyelination along medullary veins oriented perpendicular to the ependyma. Look for central vein sign/ paramagnetic rim sign on SWI
2) Active plaques show open-ring or nodular enhancement and may restrict diffusion at the leading edge; chronic "black holes" are T1-hypointense without enhancement. | Dawson fingers, Open-ring enhancement | Dawson's fingers | Multiple sclerosis | MS
explanation: Dawson’s fingers are ovoid periventricular T2/FLAIR lesions oriented perpendicular to the ventricular surface. They follow perivenular inflammatory demyelination along medullary veins. Active plaques show a broken blood-brain barrier (enhancement), whereas chronic lesions do not.
key_findings:
Dawson’s fingers: FLAIR-hyperintense, radially oriented ovoid lesions at the callosal-septal interface
Central vein sign: a small vein within the lesion on SWI/T2*
Paramagnetic rim lesions: SWI rim of iron-laden microglia, marking chronic active (smoldering) lesions
Active plaque: open-ring or nodular enhancement, with restricted diffusion at the leading edge
Chronic plaque: T1 “black hole” with no enhancement
Others: juxtacortical, infratentorial and cord lesions
learning_points:
Enhancement lasts about 4 to 6 weeks, so enhancing and non-enhancing lesions together indicate dissemination in time.
Central vein sign helps separate MS from mimics.
Open-ring enhancement (open toward the cortex) favors demyelination over abscess or tumor.
differential_diagnosis:
Small vessel ischemic disease: periventricular and subcortical white matter lesions, but spares the callosal-septal interface and has no central vein sign.
NMOSD/MOGAD: longitudinally extensive cord or optic nerve lesions, with fewer Dawson’s fingers.
ADEM: large, bilateral, ill-defined lesions, often post-infectious and monophasic.
Susac syndrome: central callosal “snowball” lesions.
Neurosarcoidosis or vasculitis: leptomeningeal enhancement or vascular territory lesions.

title: Atrial septal defect closure device
question_text:
Identify the device
What happens when the normal left to right shunt is reversed?
correct_answer:
1) Atrial septal defect (ASD) closure device (percutaneous septal occluder)
2) Eisenmenger syndrome ("Eisenmengerization"): long-standing left-to-right shunting causes pulmonary arterial hypertension and pulmonary vascular remodelling until the shunt reverses to right-to-left, causing cyanosis. | ASD closure device, Eisenmenger syndrome | Atrial septal defect closure device | Amplatzer septal occluder | ASD occluder | Eisenmenger syndrome
explanation:
The chest radiograph shows a radiopaque, double-disc device projecting over the expected position of the interatrial septum, in keeping with a transcatheter ASD occluder placed through the femoral vein.
A secundum ASD produces a left-to-right shunt at atrial level. The right heart and pulmonary circulation are volume-loaded for years, and the radiograph of an unrepaired ASD shows cardiomegaly with right atrial and ventricular enlargement, a prominent main pulmonary artery, pulmonary plethora and a small aortic knuckle.
If the shunt is left untreated, pulmonary vascular resistance rises until it exceeds systemic resistance and the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger syndrome). At that stage closure is contraindicated.
key_findings:
Metallic double-disc occluder projecting over the interatrial septum
Look for residual features of right heart volume load or pulmonary hypertension (central pulmonary artery enlargement with peripheral pruning)
learning_points:
Percutaneous device closure is suited to secundum ASDs with adequate surrounding rims. Primum, sinus venosus and coronary sinus defects are not suitable for devices and need surgery.
Eisenmenger syndrome can complicate any large left-to-right shunt (ASD, VSD, PDA). Its radiograph shows dilated central pulmonary arteries that taper abruptly, sometimes with calcification.
Follow-up for device complications: erosion, embolisation, residual shunt, and arrhythmia.
differential_diagnosis:
Patent foramen ovale occluder
Ventricular septal defect occluder or patent ductus arteriosus device
Pacemaker or ICD leads
Prosthetic valve or annuloplasty ring

title: Subclavian steal syndrome
question_text:
What is the cause of this phenomenon?
What is the expected spectral flow in the ipsilateral subclavian artery?
correct_answer:
1) Subclavian artery stenosis or obstruction proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery (most commonly atherosclerotic, left more than right)
2) Parvus et tardus flow (damped waveform with delayed upstroke), or absent flow if occluded | Proximal subclavian artery stenosis, Parvus et tardus | Subclavian steal syndrome | Subclavian artery stenosis, parvus et tardus
explanation:
Spectral Doppler of the left vertebral artery shows a waveform that alternates above and below the baseline, i.e. part antegrade and part retrograde flow. This bidirectional (alternating) pattern is an intermediate stage of subclavian steal.
With a proximal subclavian stenosis the pressure distal to it falls. Blood is then drawn retrogradely down the ipsilateral vertebral artery from the basilar circulation to supply the arm. Exercising the arm increases demand and the reversal, producing vertebrobasilar symptoms such as dizziness, visual disturbance, ataxia and syncope.
The stenotic subclavian artery shows a damped, delayed (parvus et tardus) waveform beyond the lesion.
key_findings:
Vertebral artery flow that is bidirectional or completely reversed
Damped, delayed waveform in the ipsilateral subclavian or axillary artery
Blood pressure difference of more than 15 to 20 mmHg between the two arms
Reactive hyperaemia (cuff inflation then release) increases the retrograde component
learning_points:
Stages on Doppler: (1) mid-systolic deceleration or notching of the vertebral waveform, (2) alternating antegrade and retrograde flow, (3) complete flow reversal.
Most patients with the finding are asymptomatic; "steal syndrome" implies symptoms. Treatment for symptomatic cases is angioplasty with stenting, or bypass (carotid-subclavian).
The right side is affected if the lesion involves the brachiocephalic artery.
differential_diagnosis:
Vertebral artery stenosis or dissection
Carotid or vertebrobasilar atherosclerotic disease
Takayasu arteritis (aortic arch syndrome)
Thoracic outlet syndrome
Peripheral vestibular causes of dizziness (e.g. benign paroxysmal positional vertigo)

title: Achalasia cardia
question_text:
What is the underlying pathophysiological abnormality?
What is the gold standard for diagnosis?
correct_answer:
1) Failure of lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation with loss of normal peristalsis, due to degeneration of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.
2) Manometry | Failure of LES relaxation / loss of myenteric ganglion cells, Manometry | Esophageal manometry | Achalasia cardia | Achalasia
explanation:
The barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus above a smooth, symmetrical tapering at the gastro-oesophageal junction (the "bird's beak" or "rat-tail" appearance), with retained contrast and absent effective peristalsis.
Loss of inhibitory neurons (nitric oxide and VIP releasing) leaves the LES with a high resting pressure and incomplete relaxation, and the oesophageal body loses its coordinated peristalsis. Food and secretions are retained, and the oesophagus dilates over time.
Oesophageal manometry confirms the diagnosis (high-resolution manometry with Chicago classification subtypes), while the barium swallow gives the typical morphology.
key_findings:
Dilated, sometimes sigmoid-shaped oesophagus with an air-fluid level
Smooth, tapered "bird's beak" narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction
Absent gastric air bubble on radiographs
Absent primary peristalsis, with a delay in barium emptying (timed barium swallow)
learning_points:
Always exclude pseudoachalasia (a tumour at or near the gastro-oesophageal junction mimicking achalasia). Suggestive features are older age, short symptom duration, weight loss, and an irregular or shouldered narrowing. Endoscopy and CT are used for this.
Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) causes secondary achalasia.
Treatment options include pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy, peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) and botulinum toxin injection.
differential_diagnosis:
Pseudoachalasia from a gastro-oesophageal junction carcinoma
Peptic stricture
Scleroderma (patulous, aperistaltic oesophagus with a wide-open LES)
Chagas disease
Diffuse oesophageal spasm (corkscrew oesophagus)

title: Gallstone ileus
clinical_info: 82-year-old woman with abdominal pain and distension
question_text:
What is this classic triad called?
Where does obstruction most commonly occur, and why?
correct_answer:
1) Rigler's triad: small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, and an ectopic gallstone. It results from a large stone eroding through a cholecysto-duodenal fistula and passing into the bowel.
2) The terminal ileum near the ileocaecal valve is the most common impaction site, being the narrowest part of the distal small bowel lumen. | Rigler triad, Terminal ileum | Rigler's triad | Gallstone ileus
explanation:
Coronal CT shows dilated small bowel loops with a transition point in the distal small bowel, where a rounded, laminated, calcified stone is lodged (arrow). Gas in the biliary tree (pneumobilia) is present.
Chronic gallstone disease causes inflammation and adhesion of the gallbladder to the duodenum. A large stone (typically over 2 to 2.5 cm) erodes through the wall to form a cholecysto-duodenal fistula, enters the small bowel and obstructs, most often at the terminal ileum.
The elderly woman with a history of gallstone disease is the typical patient.
key_findings:
Small bowel obstruction with dilated proximal loops and collapsed distal bowel
Pneumobilia (gas within the biliary tree)
Ectopic gallstone in the bowel lumen (often only the rim is dense, or the stone is isodense and easily missed)
Collapsed, thick-walled gallbladder, possibly containing gas, with fistula to the duodenum
learning_points:
Only about 10 to 15% of gallstones are radiopaque, so the stone is often not visible on a plain radiograph, and CT is the investigation of choice.
Bouveret syndrome is the variant in which the stone lodges in the duodenum or pylorus and produces gastric outlet obstruction.
Treatment is surgical enterolithotomy to remove the stone; cholecystectomy and fistula closure may be delayed.
differential_diagnosis:
Adhesional or hernial small bowel obstruction
Obstructing small bowel tumour
Pneumobilia from other causes: previous sphincterotomy, biliary stent or bilio-enteric anastomosis
Emphysematous cholecystitis
Other enteroliths or bezoar

title: Pneumatosis intestinalis
question_text:
What is the common cause of this appearance in neonates?
List causes of this appearance
correct_answer:
1) Necrotising enterocolitis
2) Bowel ischaemia; intestinal obstruction; toxic megacolon; benign causes such as pulmonary diseases and post-gastrointestinal interventions | Necrotising enterocolitis, Bowel ischaemia | Necrotizing enterocolitis | NEC | Pneumatosis intestinalis
explanation:
Coronal CT shows linear and bubbly collections of gas lying within the wall of the bowel, which is pneumatosis intestinalis. It is best identified on lung window settings, where the gas is clearly separate from the lumen.
Pneumatosis is an imaging sign and not a diagnosis. Its significance depends entirely on the clinical context and associated findings: in an unwell patient with bowel wall thickening, poor wall enhancement, mesenteric or portal venous gas, or ascites, it signals transmural infarction; in a well patient with a benign cause it may be an incidental finding.
key_findings:
Intramural gas in the bowel wall (linear or cystic/bubbly)
Associated portal venous gas or mesenteric venous gas
Poor wall enhancement, bowel dilatation, mesenteric stranding and free fluid suggest ischaemia
Look for SMA/SMV occlusion on contrast-enhanced CT
learning_points:
Causes of pneumatosis: bowel ischaemia, necrotising enterocolitis in neonates, bowel obstruction, toxic megacolon and inflammatory bowel disease, infection, steroids and immunosuppression, connective tissue diseases, and benign causes such as chronic obstructive lung disease and asthma, endoscopy and other gastrointestinal interventions.
Cystic or bubbly pneumatosis (particularly in the colon) is more often benign and chronic, whereas linear pneumatosis is more often associated with ischaemia, but the pattern alone is unreliable and clinical correlation is essential.
differential_diagnosis:
Pseudopneumatosis: gas trapped between faeces and wall, or between folds
Intraluminal gas bubbles within stool
Pneumoperitoneum or gas in an adjacent diverticulum
Emphysematous gastritis or enteritis

title: Ovarian teratoma (dermoid cyst)
clinical_info: 34-year-old woman with an incidental adnexal mass
question_text:
What germ layers contribute to this tumour's tissue, and what is the significance of the Rokitansky nodule?
In a localised lesion, what imaging characteristic favours malignant nature?
correct_answer:
1) Composed of tissue from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). The Rokitansky nodule (dermoid plug) is a solid protuberance projecting from the cyst wall that contains hair, fat, teeth or bone, and it is the usual site from which malignant transformation (most often squamous cell carcinoma) arises.
2) Solid enhancing components | Ectoderm mesoderm endoderm, Rokitansky nodule, Solid enhancing components | Mature cystic teratoma | Ovarian dermoid cyst | Ovarian teratoma | Dermoid cyst
explanation:
A mature cystic teratoma is a well-defined adnexal cystic mass containing fat, which is T1-hyperintense and loses signal on fat-suppressed sequences. It may show a fat-fluid level, a Rokitansky nodule projecting into the lumen, and calcification or teeth.
MRI confirms the fat content, demonstrates the nodule, and assesses for solid enhancing tissue, which would raise the possibility of malignant transformation.
key_findings:
Fat within an adnexal cyst (T1 hyperintense, suppressed on fat saturation)
Rokitansky nodule or dermoid plug projecting from the wall
Fat-fluid level; possible calcification or tooth
Solid enhancing components, wall invasion or extension beyond the ovary suggest malignancy
learning_points:
Most common ovarian germ cell tumour and the most common benign ovarian neoplasm in young women. Bilateral in about 10 to 15%.
Complications: torsion (most frequent), rupture with chemical peritonitis, infection, and malignant transformation in about 1 to 2%, mostly in older women.
Teratomas are associated with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, so a young woman with this encephalitis warrants a search for an ovarian teratoma.
differential_diagnosis:
Endometrioma: T1 hyperintense but T2 shading, and persists on fat suppression
Haemorrhagic cyst
Immature teratoma: large, predominantly solid mass in a young patient with scattered calcification and small foci of fat
Struma ovarii
Mucinous cystadenoma

title: Staghorn calculus (struvite)
question_text:
What is the most common underlying infectious cause?
What is the typical stone composition?
correct_answer:
1) Chronic infection by urease-producing organisms (Proteus mirabilis) that alkalinise the urine.
2) Most staghorn calculi are struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate). | Proteus mirabilis, Struvite | Magnesium ammonium phosphate | Proteus, Struvite | Staghorn calculus
explanation:
The abdominal radiograph shows a dense, branching calcification in the left renal area forming a cast of the pelvicalyceal system (a staghorn calculus).
Urease-producing organisms (classically Proteus mirabilis, also Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Providencia and Staphylococcus saprophyticus) split urea to ammonia, which alkalinises the urine and drives precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and carbonate apatite. Escherichia coli does not produce urease.
key_findings:
Branching radiodense calculus occupying the renal pelvis and extending into the calyces
Possible hydronephrosis, cortical thinning and a small or non-functioning kidney on follow-up imaging
learning_points:
Struvite stones are typically moderately radiopaque, form in infected alkaline urine, and are commoner in women with recurrent urinary tract infections.
Complete removal (percutaneous nephrolithotomy, often combined with other modalities) is needed because residual fragments harbour bacteria and perpetuate infection. Untreated cases may progress to pyonephrosis, xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis and loss of the kidney.
CT without contrast is used to define the stone burden, and a functional study (DMSA or MAG3) assesses renal function before deciding on surgery.
differential_diagnosis:
Large calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate stones
Cystine stone (faintly opaque, ground-glass)
Uric acid stone (radiolucent)
Renal tuberculosis with calcification (autonephrectomy)
Nephrocalcinosis

title: Horseshoe kidney
question_text:
Name the sign.
What structure prevents the kidneys from ascending?
correct_answer:
1) Flower-vase sign, due to medially directed lower calyces.
2) The isthmus is typically trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent. | Flower-vase sign, Inferior mesenteric artery | Flower vase sign, IMA | Horseshoe kidney
explanation:
There is low-lying position of both kidneys, with the lower poles directed medially and the lower calyces pointing toward the midline, giving the flower-vase (drooping lily) appearance. The lower poles are joined by an isthmus across the midline.
Horseshoe kidney is the commonest renal fusion anomaly. The isthmus lies anterior to the aorta and IVC, usually at the L3-L4 level, and is held back by the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent. Incomplete rotation leaves the renal pelves facing anteriorly, and the ureters pass over the isthmus with a high insertion on the pelvis. The resulting poor drainage predisposes to stones, infection and pelviureteric junction obstruction.
key_findings:
Kidneys lying low with the long axes converging inferiorly (in contrast to the normal axis)
Lower poles fused across the midline by an isthmus of parenchyma or fibrous tissue
Medially directed lower calyces (flower-vase sign) and anteriorly facing renal pelves
Calculi, hydronephrosis or recurrent infection as complications
learning_points:
CT (or MRI) demonstrates the isthmus clearly, as well as the vascular supply, which is variable and often multiple.
Associations: Turner syndrome and trisomy 18. Increased incidence of Wilms tumour and renal carcinoid, and the usual renal tumours.
The isthmus is usually left in place at surgery, but the variable and often multiple renal arteries matter for any intervention.
differential_diagnosis:
Crossed fused renal ectopia
Pelvic kidney
Malrotated kidneys without fusion
Retroperitoneal mass or nodes overlying the great vessels (on cross-sectional imaging)

title: Complete hydatidiform mole
question_text:
What is the karyotype and mechanism of formation of a complete hydatidiform mole?
What pathognomonic change can be seen in the ovaries?
correct_answer:
1) A complete mole typically arises from fertilisation of an empty ovum, usually resulting in a diploid, entirely paternal karyotype (46,XX), with no fetal tissue.
2) Theca lutein cysts | 46,XX diploid paternal, Theca lutein cysts | 46 XX, Theca lutein cysts | Complete hydatidiform mole | Hydatidiform mole
explanation:
Pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged uterine cavity filled with a heterogeneous echogenic mass containing numerous small anechoic cystic spaces, the "snowstorm" or "cluster of grapes" pattern, without a recognisable fetus or gestational sac.
In a complete mole an enucleate egg is fertilised by a single haploid sperm that duplicates its chromosomes (46,XX), or occasionally by two sperms (46,XY or XX). All the genetic material is paternal, so there is no embryo, and the chorionic villi undergo diffuse hydropic swelling with trophoblastic proliferation.
The β-hCG is markedly elevated, and high levels cause bilateral enlarged multiloculated ovaries (theca lutein cysts).
key_findings:
Absent fetus with diffusely enlarged uterus filled by vesicular, echogenic tissue
Bilateral theca lutein cysts (multiloculated enlarged ovaries) from β-hCG stimulation
Markedly elevated β-hCG, often with hyperemesis and early pre-eclampsia
Increased vascularity on Doppler
learning_points:
A partial mole is triploid (69,XXX or 69,XXY: two paternal and one maternal set), contains fetal tissue, and shows a thickened cystic placenta with an abnormal fetus.
Complete moles carry a risk of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia of around 15 to 20% (partial moles about 1 to 5%). Treatment is suction curettage with serial β-hCG follow-up. Chest imaging is used to look for lung metastases if the β-hCG fails to fall.
Invasive mole and choriocarcinoma are the malignant sequelae.
differential_diagnosis:
Partial hydatidiform mole
Missed or incomplete miscarriage with hydropic degeneration
Twin pregnancy with a complete mole and a coexisting normal fetus
Degenerating fibroid
Placental mesenchymal dysplasia

title: Caroli disease
clinical_info: 16-year-old with recurrent right upper quadrant pain, fever and jaundice
question_text:
What is the "central dot sign," and what structure does it represent?
What results when combined with congenital hepatic fibrosis, and what associated renal condition is seen?
correct_answer:
1) It represents portal vein radicles (with hepatic artery branches) surrounded by, and partially engulfed within, the dilated intrahepatic bile ducts.
2) Combined with congenital hepatic fibrosis, the condition is termed Caroli syndrome, frequently associated with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. | Portal vein radicle within dilated bile duct, Caroli syndrome, ARPKD | Central dot sign, Caroli syndrome | Caroli disease | Caroli syndrome
explanation:
The MRCP shows multiple saccular and cystic dilatations of the intrahepatic bile ducts that communicate with the biliary tree. Their "beaded" appearance is characteristic.
Caroli disease is a congenital communicating cystic dilatation of the segmental intrahepatic bile ducts (a Todani type V choledochal cyst). Bile stasis predisposes to stones, sludge, recurrent cholangitis and liver abscesses, which explain the fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice.
On contrast-enhanced CT, MRI or ultrasound, the portal vein radicle with its accompanying hepatic artery is seen as an enhancing dot within the dilated duct, the central dot sign.
key_findings:
Multiple saccular dilatations of intrahepatic bile ducts communicating with the biliary tree
Central dot sign: enhancing portal radicle within a dilated duct
Intraductal stones or sludge and signs of cholangitis
Associated renal tubular ectasia or cysts
learning_points:
Caroli disease is autosomal recessive (PKHD1 gene). Caroli syndrome (Caroli disease with congenital hepatic fibrosis) presents with portal hypertension, and is typically associated with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease or medullary sponge kidney-like tubular ectasia.
The lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma is increased (about 7%).
differential_diagnosis:
Polycystic liver disease: cysts do not communicate with the biliary tree and show no central dot sign
Recurrent pyogenic (oriental) cholangitis: dilated extrahepatic ducts with stones
Primary sclerosing cholangitis: strictures with beading, but not saccular dilatation
Biliary hamartomas (von Meyenburg complexes)
Multiple hepatic abscesses

title: Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH)
clinical_info: 32-year-old asymptomatic woman with an incidental liver lesion
question_text:
What are the characteristics of the central scar on MRI?
What scintigraphic tests help in diagnosis?
correct_answer:
1) T2-hyperintense central scar (fibrolamellar HCC: T2-hypointense scar).
2) Tc-99m sulfur colloid is taken up by the normal Kupffer cells within the lesion, and HIDA (hepatobiliary scintigraphy) is excreted by hepatocytes. | T2-hyperintense central scar, Tc-99m sulfur colloid / HIDA | T2 hyperintense scar, Sulfur colloid | Focal nodular hyperplasia | FNH
explanation:
Multiphase CT shows a well-defined lesion that enhances intensely and homogeneously in the arterial phase, except for a central scar, and becomes isodense to the surrounding liver in the portal venous and delayed phases. The central scar enhances on delayed images.
FNH is a hyperplastic response to a pre-existing arterial malformation, and is composed of normal hepatocytes, Kupffer cells and bile ductules in abnormal arrangement with a central fibrous scar.
key_findings:
Arterial hyperenhancement that becomes isodense on portal and delayed phases
Central stellate scar, T2-hyperintense on MRI, with delayed enhancement
No capsule, haemorrhage, necrosis or calcification
Hepatobiliary-phase MRI agents (gadoxetate/gadobenate): iso- to hyperintense lesion, in contrast to adenoma
learning_points:
FNH has no malignant potential and generally requires no treatment, so the key role of imaging is to confirm the diagnosis and avoid biopsy or surgery.
Many FNH lesions show normal or increased sulfur colloid uptake because they contain Kupffer cells (adenomas and metastases usually do not), and HIDA shows uptake with delayed excretion.
Typical patient: woman of reproductive age.
differential_diagnosis:
Hepatic adenoma: fat or haemorrhage, no scar, hypointense on hepatobiliary phase
Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma: large, calcification, T2-hypointense scar, young adult
Hepatocellular carcinoma (in a cirrhotic liver, with washout)
Hypervascular metastasis
Haemangioma: peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement

title: Thyroglossal duct cyst
clinical_info: 6-year-old girl with painless neck swelling moving with deglutition
question_text:
What developmental tract does this lesion arise from, and what is its most common location relative to the hyoid?
Why must normal thyroid tissue be confirmed before surgical excision?
correct_answer:
1) Origin: remnant of the thyroglossal duct tracking from the foramen caecum to the normal thyroid position; most commonly midline or paramedian, infrahyoid or at the hyoid level.
2) It may harbour ectopic thyroid tissue or, rarely, papillary carcinoma. A normally located thyroid must be confirmed, as the cyst may be the patient's only functioning thyroid tissue. | Thyroglossal duct, Infrahyoid midline, Confirm normal thyroid / ectopic thyroid | Thyroglossal duct cyst
explanation:
Ultrasound of the neck shows a well-defined, anechoic or hypoechoic cystic lesion in the midline at the level of the hyoid bone, with posterior acoustic enhancement. Internal echoes or a thick wall suggest infection.
The thyroglossal duct is the embryologic tract along which the thyroid descends from the foramen caecum to the lower neck. Persistence of part of the tract gives a cyst that moves upward on swallowing and on tongue protrusion because it is attached to the hyoid via the tract.
key_findings:
Midline cystic neck mass at or just below the hyoid, embedded in the strap muscles when infrahyoid
May show a tract extending toward the hyoid
Solid mural nodule or calcification raises the possibility of papillary carcinoma
Ultrasound should confirm a normal thyroid gland in its usual location
learning_points:
The Sistrunk procedure removes the cyst together with the central portion of the hyoid bone and the tract up to the foramen caecum, which minimises recurrence.
The commonest malignancy arising in a thyroglossal duct cyst is papillary thyroid carcinoma (under 1% of cysts).
Infection is common and may mimic an abscess.
differential_diagnosis:
Dermoid or epidermoid cyst (submental or midline)
Lymph node or reactive adenopathy
Lingual or ectopic thyroid
Branchial cleft cyst (lateral neck)
Lymphatic malformation, laryngocele or thymic cyst

title: Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumour)
clinical_info: 70-year-old man with progressive painless jaundice and pale stools
question_text:
What classification describes tumour extent relative to the biliary confluence, and why does it matter for surgery?
What are the different growth patterns of this lesion?
correct_answer:
1) The Bismuth-Corlette classification describes ductal involvement at the confluence, directly informing resectability and the extent of hepatic resection.
2) Mass-forming; periductal-infiltrating; intraductal-growing. | Bismuth-Corlette classification; Mass-forming, periductal-infiltrating, intraductal-growing | Bismuth-Corlette | Klatskin tumour | Hilar cholangiocarcinoma
explanation:
The cholangiogram shows dilated intrahepatic ducts with a stricture at the hilum and a failure of the right and left hepatic ducts to communicate at the confluence, with abrupt cut-off of contrast.
Hilar cholangiocarcinoma arises at or near the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts. Obstructive jaundice with pale stools and dark urine in an older man is the typical presentation.
The Bismuth-Corlette types are: I, tumour below the confluence (the right and left ducts still communicate); II, involving the confluence with no communication; IIIa, extending into the right hepatic duct; IIIb, extending into the left hepatic duct; IV, extending into both or multifocal.
key_findings:
Hilar duct stricture with proximal dilatation and non-union of the right and left hepatic ducts
Periductal thickening or infiltrating mass at the hilum
Lobar atrophy with contralateral hypertrophy
Portal vein or hepatic artery encasement and nodal metastases affect resectability
learning_points:
Risk factors include primary sclerosing cholangitis, liver flukes (Opisthorchis, Clonorchis), choledochal cysts and hepatolithiasis. CA 19-9 is raised but not specific.
The periductal-infiltrating type is the commonest morphology of hilar tumours and is often hard to see on cross-sectional imaging, so MRCP combined with contrast MRI or CT is used for staging.
Unresectable disease includes bilateral secondary biliary radicle involvement, bilateral vascular involvement and distant metastases.
differential_diagnosis:
Dominant stricture in primary sclerosing cholangitis
IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis
Mirizzi syndrome
Gallbladder carcinoma invading the hilum
Metastatic periportal nodes

title: Hydroxyapatite deposition disease (calcific tendinitis)
question_text:
What is the most common site of this lesion?
What treatment procedure involves ultrasound-guided lavage?
correct_answer:
1) Supraspinatus tendon
2) Barbotage | Supraspinatus tendon, Barbotage | Supraspinatus, Barbotage | Calcific tendinitis | Hydroxyapatite deposition disease | HADD
explanation:
The shoulder radiograph (internal rotation view) shows calcific deposits in the soft tissues adjacent to the greater tuberosity, in keeping with calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff.
Hydroxyapatite deposition disease (HADD) is deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals in tendons, most commonly in the supraspinatus about 1 to 2 cm proximal to its insertion (the critical zone). The condition passes through formative, resorptive and post-calcific stages. The resorptive phase is the most painful, and the deposit then looks fluffy and ill-defined and may rupture into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa.
key_findings:
Dense, homogeneous or fluffy calcification in the rotator cuff tendon, usually above the humeral head
Internal and external rotation views help to localise the deposit
Ultrasound shows hyperechoic foci with or without shadowing and hyperaemia in the resorptive phase
MRI: low signal on all sequences with surrounding oedema
learning_points:
Barbotage is ultrasound-guided needle lavage that breaks up and aspirates the calcific deposit, usually with a corticosteroid injection. Other treatments are NSAIDs, physiotherapy, extracorporeal shock wave therapy and arthroscopic removal.
The condition is self-limiting in most patients, and typically occurs between 30 and 50 years of age, with a female predominance.
The resorptive phase can mimic infection or a tumour, so clinical correlation is important.
differential_diagnosis:
Calcific tendinitis of other tendons (infraspinatus, subscapularis)
Calcified loose body or ossicle
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis (when ill-defined in the resorptive phase)
Myositis ossificans or tumoral calcinosis

title: Fibroadenoma
question_text:
What characteristic calcification is depicted?
Name characteristic ultrasound features when the lesion is non-calcified.
correct_answer:
1) Popcorn calcifications
2) Wider than tall (oval); hypoechoic; macrolobulations; posterior acoustic enhancement. | Popcorn calcifications; Oval wider-than-tall hypoechoic macrolobulated | Popcorn calcification | Fibroadenoma
explanation:
The mammogram shows several coarse, dense, "popcorn" calcifications within the breast, typical of involuting (degenerating) fibroadenomas.
A fibroadenoma is the commonest benign breast tumour in young women. On ultrasound a non-calcified fibroadenoma is an oval, circumscribed, hypoechoic mass with its long axis parallel to the skin (wider than tall), a few gentle macrolobulations, a thin echogenic capsule, and posterior acoustic enhancement.
key_findings:
Coarse (popcorn) calcifications within a circumscribed mass on mammography
Ultrasound: oval, wider-than-tall, circumscribed, hypoechoic mass with macrolobulations and posterior enhancement
Often multiple and bilateral
learning_points:
A typical mammographic or ultrasound fibroadenoma is classified as BI-RADS 2 or 3 according to the findings, and may be followed rather than biopsied if features are classic and the patient is young.
Rapid growth, large size (over 5 cm) or irregular features should raise the possibility of a phyllodes tumour, and biopsy is then needed.
Popcorn calcification is coarse, large and stable; fine pleomorphic or linear branching calcification suggests malignancy.
differential_diagnosis:
Phyllodes tumour (rapid growth, larger, cystic clefts)
Simple or complicated cyst
Intraductal papilloma
Fat necrosis or calcified oil cyst
Malignant calcification (fine, pleomorphic, linear branching)

title: Vertebra plana (Langerhans cell histiocytosis)
question_text:
What is the most common cause of this appearance in children?
Name the triad of skull defects, exophthalmos and diabetes insipidus seen in multisystemic involvement.
correct_answer:
1) Eosinophilic granuloma / Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH)
2) Hand-Schüller-Christian disease | Langerhans cell histiocytosis / Eosinophilic granuloma, Hand-Schuller-Christian disease | Eosinophilic granuloma, Hand-Schuller-Christian | Langerhans cell histiocytosis | LCH | Vertebra plana
explanation:
The lateral radiograph shows near-complete collapse of a vertebral body into a thin wafer ("coin on edge"), with preservation of the adjacent intervertebral disc spaces and posterior elements.
Vertebra plana in a child with back pain is most commonly caused by the solitary (unifocal) form of LCH, formerly eosinophilic granuloma. The disc spaces are normally preserved, which helps to separate it from infection. The collapsed vertebra often re-expands partly over time.
key_findings:
Uniform flattening of one vertebral body (vertebra plana) with normal adjacent discs
Possible small associated soft tissue mass without cord compression
Lytic lesions in the skull, mandible and long bones in multifocal disease
learning_points:
LCH is classified as single-system (unifocal or multifocal) or multisystem. Hand-Schüller-Christian disease is the chronic multifocal form with the triad of skull defects (lytic "geographic skull"), exophthalmos and diabetes insipidus. Letterer-Siwe disease is the acute disseminated form of infancy with visceral involvement.
Most spinal LCH is managed conservatively, with steroid injection or chemotherapy in selected cases.
differential_diagnosis:
Ewing sarcoma
Leukaemia or lymphoma
Osteomyelitis or discitis (the disc is involved)
Metastasis (e.g. neuroblastoma)
Traumatic compression fracture or metabolic bone disease (osteogenesis imperfecta, Gaucher)

title: Diffuse axonal injury
clinical_info: History of motor vehicle accident with normal CT
question_text:
What MRI sequence has the highest sensitivity for this pathology?
How is this pathology graded?
correct_answer:
1) Gradient-echo / susceptibility-weighted sequences are the most sensitive for detection of microbleeds.
2) Grade I: microhaemorrhages limited to the grey-white matter junction. Grade II: Grade I plus corpus callosum. Grade III: Grade I and II plus brainstem. | SWI / GRE, Adams grading (grey-white, corpus callosum, brainstem) | Susceptibility-weighted imaging | SWI | Diffuse axonal injury | DAI
explanation:
SWI shows multiple small foci of signal loss (microhaemorrhages) at the grey-white matter junctions, consistent with shear injury, even though the initial CT was normal.
Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) results from rotational acceleration-deceleration forces that shear axons at interfaces between tissues of different density. Typical locations are the grey-white junction (parasagittal frontal and temporal lobes), the corpus callosum (especially the splenium) and the dorsolateral brainstem. Many lesions are non-haemorrhagic and are only seen on DWI or FLAIR.
key_findings:
Multiple small haemorrhagic foci at the grey-white junction, corpus callosum, and brainstem
Non-haemorrhagic lesions: restricted diffusion and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity
CT is frequently normal or shows only small petechial haemorrhages
learning_points:
The number and location of lesions correlate with the clinical outcome, and brainstem involvement (grade III) carries a poor prognosis.
SWI is more sensitive than T2*-gradient echo, and sensitivity improves with field strength. DWI should be added for non-haemorrhagic lesions.
differential_diagnosis:
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy and hypertensive microbleeds (typical distribution and age)
Cavernous malformations (multiple, sometimes familial)
Fat embolism (starfield pattern on DWI)
Haemorrhagic metastases (e.g. melanoma) or septic emboli
Hypoxic-ischaemic injury

title: Inferior vena cava (IVC) filter placement
clinical_info: 68-year-old man with acute femoral vein thrombosis
question_text:
What is the primary indication for this device?
What complication is associated with prolonged indwelling time of a retrievable device left beyond the recommended window?
correct_answer:
1) Indicated for PE prevention in patients with venous thromboembolism who have an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation.
2) Prolonged dwell time increases risk of tilting, fracture, migration and caval penetration, and increases difficulty of percutaneous retrieval. | Contraindication to anticoagulation in VTE, Tilting / fracture / migration / caval penetration | IVC filter | Inferior vena cava filter
explanation:
The cavogram shows a conical filter with several legs deployed in the infrarenal IVC, with the apex of the filter directed cranially, positioned to trap emboli travelling from the lower limb veins towards the lungs.
IVC filters are used in patients with acute proximal deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism in whom anticoagulation is contraindicated, has failed or has caused a serious complication. They do not treat the thrombosis itself and should be retrieved as soon as the contraindication has resolved.
key_findings:
Filter deployed in the infrarenal IVC with its apex cranial
Check for tilt (over 15°), strut fracture, caval penetration and filter thrombus
Contrast venography is performed before placement to define IVC size and renal vein levels
learning_points:
Retrievable filters should be removed early (regulatory guidance suggests within about 1 to 2 months once the PE risk has passed). Long dwell times increase complications such as caval wall penetration, strut fracture with embolisation, IVC thrombosis and post-thrombotic syndrome.
Prophylactic placement in patients without VTE has limited evidence.
differential_diagnosis:
Other filter types and appearances (Greenfield, Günther Tulip, Celect, OptEase)
Caval thrombosis around the filter
Filter migration or fracture with fragment embolisation

title: Vein of Galen malformation
question_text:
As per Lasjaunias classification, what are the two types?
What is the common clinical manifestation when it presents in a neonate?
correct_answer:
1) Choroidal and mural
2) High-output cardiac failure | Choroidal and mural, High-output cardiac failure | Choroidal and mural | Vein of Galen malformation
explanation:
The sagittal T2-weighted MRI shows a markedly dilated, flow-void-containing midline venous pouch behind the third ventricle above the tectal plate, which is the aneurysmal vein of Galen malformation, together with ventricular dilatation (hydrocephalus).
A vein of Galen malformation is an arteriovenous shunt draining into the embryonic median prosencephalic vein of Markowski, which dilates because of the high flow. It is not a true malformation of the vein of Galen itself.
In a neonate the massive shunt causes high-output cardiac failure. In infants it causes hydrocephalus and macrocrania with prominent scalp veins, and in older children developmental delay, headaches, or haemorrhage.
key_findings:
Dilated midline venous pouch with flow voids posterior to the third ventricle
Dilated feeding arteries (choroidal, quadrigeminal, anterior cerebral branches)
Hydrocephalus; parenchymal atrophy or calcification from chronic venous hypertension
learning_points:
The Lasjaunias classification divides vein of Galen malformations into the choroidal type, with multiple feeders converging on the venous pouch (usually presenting in the neonate with heart failure), and the mural type, with one or a few direct fistulae into the wall of the pouch (presenting in infancy or childhood).
Treatment is staged transarterial endovascular embolisation, usually timed by cardiac status and age, and the Bicêtre score guides neonatal management.
differential_diagnosis:
Dural sinus malformations
Arteriovenous malformation draining into the vein of Galen (galenic drainage)
Pineal or arachnoid cyst
Pineal region tumour

title: Endobronchial intubation
question_text:
What is the cause of white-out of the left hemithorax?
What radiograph landmarks can be used in this scenario?
correct_answer:
1) Left lung atelectasis (collapse), due to the endotracheal tube lying in the right main bronchus
2) Clavicular heads and carina | Left lung collapse / atelectasis from right mainstem intubation, Carina and clavicular heads | Right main bronchus intubation, Left lung collapse | Endobronchial intubation
explanation:
The portable chest radiograph shows the tip of the endotracheal tube below the carina in the right main bronchus, with opacification of the whole left hemithorax from lung collapse and volume loss, while the right lung is hyperinflated.
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so a tube advanced too far usually enters it. The left lung is then not ventilated, and it collapses, giving a white-out with ipsilateral shift of the mediastinum.
key_findings:
Endotracheal tube tip below the carina or in the right main bronchus
Complete opacification of the left hemithorax with mediastinal shift toward the collapsed side
Hyperinflation of the right lung (risk of right pneumothorax)
learning_points:
The correct tip position is about 5 cm above the carina (range 3 to 7 cm), roughly at the level of the clavicular heads, with the neck in neutral position. Neck flexion moves the tip down by about 2 cm, and extension moves it up.
Every ICU film should also check the nasogastric tube, central lines, and for pneumothorax.
differential_diagnosis:
Massive pleural effusion (opaque hemithorax with contralateral shift)
Pneumonectomy or lung agenesis (ipsilateral shift)
Lobar pneumonia or mucus plug causing collapse
Large central tumour with lung collapse

title: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
clinical_info: 58-year-old woman with progressive altered sensorium and startle myoclonus over 4 weeks
question_text:
What is the most sensitive imaging sequence, and what other tests support the diagnosis?
What key differential must be excluded given overlapping cortical DWI changes?
correct_answer:
1) DWI is most sensitive (cortical ribboning and basal ganglia restricted diffusion). Supporting tests: CSF 14-3-3 protein, CSF or olfactory mucosa real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) seeding assays, and CSF tau.
2) The differential includes hypoxic-ischaemic injury, post-ictal change, and mitochondrial encephalopathy (e.g. MELAS); rapid progression and symmetry favour CJD. | DWI, CSF RT-QuIC / 14-3-3, Hypoxic-ischaemic / post-ictal / MELAS | Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease | Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease | sCJD | CJD
explanation:
DWI shows restricted diffusion in the cerebral cortex (cortical ribboning) and in the caudate nuclei and putamina, with corresponding low ADC values.
Sporadic CJD is a prion disease with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia and visual or cerebellar signs, usually with a fatal course in months. The characteristic imaging changes are cortical and deep grey nuclei diffusion restriction, and these may be seen before EEG and CSF changes.
key_findings:
Cortical ribboning on DWI, often asymmetric
Restricted diffusion in the caudate and putamen
FLAIR hyperintensity in the same regions, no enhancement and no significant mass effect
Variant CJD: pulvinar sign (thalamic hyperintensity)
learning_points:
Diagnostic criteria incorporate MRI, EEG (periodic sharp wave complexes) and CSF assays. RT-QuIC has a very high specificity.
Subacute presentation of rapidly progressive dementia should prompt MRI with DWI to evaluate for prion disease and autoimmune or infectious mimics.
differential_diagnosis:
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
Post-ictal change (usually transient and reversible)
MELAS and other mitochondrial disease (lesions crossing vascular territories)
Autoimmune or viral encephalitis
Hypoglycaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning or Wernicke encephalopathy

title: Pneumothorax
question_text:
What imaging features are seen on ultrasound?
What radiographic finding would indicate a life-threatening tension variant?
correct_answer:
1) Loss of pleural sliding (barcode sign on M-mode); absent B-lines; lung point (transition between air-filled and normal pleura).
2) Contralateral mediastinal shift, ipsilateral hemidiaphragm flattening or inversion, and widened rib spaces. | Absent lung sliding / barcode sign / lung point, Contralateral mediastinal shift | Barcode sign, Tension pneumothorax | Pneumothorax
explanation:
The chest radiograph shows a visible visceral pleural line with an absence of lung markings beyond it, in keeping with pneumothorax. The M-mode ultrasound tracing shows the "barcode" (stratosphere) sign, with horizontal lines throughout, instead of the normal "seashore" sign, indicating absent pleural sliding.
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically affects tall, thin young men and results from rupture of apical subpleural blebs.
key_findings:
Visceral pleural line separated from the chest wall with no peripheral lung markings
Ultrasound: absent lung sliding, absent B-lines, lung point (pathognomonic)
Tension: contralateral mediastinal shift, flattening or inversion of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, wide intercostal spaces
learning_points:
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression. Radiographic signs should not delay treatment.
Ultrasound is more sensitive than a supine chest radiograph. A deep sulcus sign is seen on supine films.
CT can identify blebs or underlying lung disease, and is used in recurrent cases.
differential_diagnosis:
Skin fold (the line extends beyond the thorax and lung markings are visible beyond it)
Giant bulla or cystic lung disease
Medial border of the scapula
Swyer-James syndrome or lobar emphysema

title: Sigmoid volvulus
clinical_info: 78-year-old with chronic constipation and progressive abdominal distension
question_text:
What sign is shown?
What is first-line management if there is no ischaemia or perforation?
correct_answer:
1) The "coffee bean" sign reflects the two apposed walls of the twisted, dilated loop; a tapered "bird's beak" at the torsion site is best seen on contrast enema or CT.
2) Endoscopic detorsion (with rectal tube) is first-line. Definitive sigmoid resection is often still needed to prevent recurrence. | Coffee bean sign, Endoscopic detorsion | Coffee bean sign | Sigmoid volvulus
explanation:
The abdominal radiograph shows a massively distended, gas-filled sigmoid loop rising out of the pelvis toward the upper abdomen, shaped like an inverted U or coffee bean with the cleft formed by the apposed medial walls of the loop.
Sigmoid volvulus is a closed-loop obstruction occurring when the sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery. It affects elderly, institutionalised or neuropsychiatric patients with chronic constipation, and in endemic regions Chagas disease.
key_findings:
Dilated inverted-U loop without haustra (coffee bean sign)
Loop apex projecting to the right upper quadrant or beyond the transverse colon
CT: whirl sign of the mesentery and a tapered bird's beak at the point of torsion
Look for ischaemia (wall thickening, pneumatosis, free fluid) or perforation
learning_points:
Flexible sigmoidoscopic detorsion with rectal tube placement is first-line if there is no gangrene or perforation. Recurrence is common (up to about half), and elective sigmoid resection is recommended in fit patients.
Emergency surgery is required for ischaemia or perforation.
differential_diagnosis:
Caecal volvulus (coffee bean in the left upper quadrant, small bowel dilatation)
Megacolon or toxic colitis
Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)
Obstructing sigmoid carcinoma

title: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
question_text:
What is the sign and its pathophysiological basis here?
What diagnostic and therapeutic procedure confirms and treats this condition?
correct_answer:
1) Crazy-paving: surfactant accumulation within alveoli combined with thickened interlobular septa.
2) Bronchoalveolar lavage is both diagnostic (milky, PAS-positive fluid) and the mainstay of treatment (whole-lung lavage). GM-CSF therapy is used in autoimmune PAP. | Crazy-paving, Bronchoalveolar lavage / whole-lung lavage | Crazy paving pattern, Whole lung lavage | Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis | PAP
explanation:
HRCT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with superimposed smooth interlobular septal thickening and intralobular lines in a polygonal "crazy-paving" pattern, with sharply demarcated normal lobules (geographic distribution).
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) is due to impaired clearance of surfactant from the alveoli, most commonly from autoantibodies against GM-CSF (autoimmune PAP). Patients may have only mild symptoms despite extensive radiological abnormality.
key_findings:
Crazy-paving pattern: ground-glass opacity with septal and intralobular thickening
Geographic distribution with sharp borders to normal lung
Clinical-radiological dissociation (mild symptoms, extensive CT changes)
learning_points:
Causes: autoimmune (about 90%), secondary (haematological malignancy, dust or chemical inhalation, infection), and congenital (surfactant gene mutations).
Complications include secondary infection (Nocardia, mycobacteria and fungi).
Crazy-paving is non-specific, and the context matters.
differential_diagnosis:
Pulmonary oedema
Viral pneumonia (e.g. COVID-19) or Pneumocystis pneumonia
Alveolar haemorrhage
Lipoid pneumonia
Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma, sarcoidosis or NSIP

title: Testicular epidermoid cyst
question_text:
What is the other name of this lesion?
What is the most common primary tumour of the testes?
correct_answer:
1) Keratocyst
2) Seminoma | Keratocyst, Seminoma | Testicular epidermoid cyst | Epidermoid cyst
explanation:
Ultrasound of the right testicle shows a well-circumscribed round intratesticular mass with concentric alternating hypoechoic and hyperechoic rings, the "onion-ring" or target appearance, caused by lamellated keratin.
An epidermoid cyst is a benign germ cell lesion lined by keratinising squamous epithelium and filled with keratin debris. It lacks internal vascularity on Doppler, which helps to distinguish it from solid tumours.
key_findings:
Round, well-defined intratesticular mass with onion-ring (laminated) pattern
Echogenic calcified rim in some cases
No internal vascularity on colour Doppler
Normal tumour markers
learning_points:
Epidermoid cysts account for roughly 1 to 2% of testicular masses. Testis-sparing enucleation is possible when imaging is typical and tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH) are normal.
Seminoma is the commonest primary testicular tumour overall: a homogeneous, hypoechoic, vascular mass in men aged 30 to 40.
differential_diagnosis:
Teratoma (heterogeneous, cystic and calcified)
Seminoma or mixed germ cell tumour
Abscess or haematoma
Burned-out germ cell tumour with scar
Simple cyst or tunica albuginea cyst

title: Hydatid cyst
question_text:
What mechanism results in the water-lily sign?
What is the characteristic difference between such a cyst when it occurs in the liver versus the lung?
correct_answer:
1) The inner endocyst separates from the outer pericyst and appears as a free-floating membrane within the cyst.
2) Hepatic cysts frequently calcify, whereas pulmonary cysts rarely calcify. | Detachment of endocyst from pericyst, Liver cysts calcify whereas lung cysts rarely calcify | Water-lily sign | Hydatid cyst | Echinococcal cyst
explanation:
CT shows a large, well-defined, low-attenuation cystic mass in the liver containing multiple smaller peripheral daughter cysts, giving a "cyst within a cyst" or rosette appearance.
Hydatid disease is caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. The liver (about 70%) and lung (about 20%) are the commonest sites. The cyst has an outer pericyst (host reaction), a laminated membrane and an inner germinal layer (endocyst). Detachment of the endocyst from the pericyst gives the floating membrane (water-lily or camalote sign) and is a sign of cyst degeneration or rupture.
key_findings:
Large unilocular or multilocular hepatic cyst with daughter cysts
Wall calcification (commonly in the liver) and floating membranes (water-lily sign)
