Complications: rupture into the biliary tree (cholangitis), peritoneum (anaphylaxis) or infection
learning_points:
The WHO-IWGE ultrasound classification (CE1 to CE5) stages the cyst and guides treatment.
Treatment options: albendazole, PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, re-aspiration), and surgery for complicated cysts.
Echinococcus multilocularis causes an infiltrative, tumour-like lesion.
differential_diagnosis:
Simple hepatic cyst
Pyogenic or amoebic liver abscess
Cystic metastases or biliary cystadenoma
Mesenchymal hamartoma or undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma (paediatric)
Choledochal cyst

title: Pentalogy of Cantrell
question_text:
What is the most commonly associated chromosomal abnormality?
Name the features of the pentalogy of Cantrell.
correct_answer:
1) Trisomy 18
2) Omphalocele; diaphragmatic defect; cardiovascular abnormalities (ASD/VSD/left ventricular diverticulum); ectopia cordis; pericardial defect or sternal cleft. | Trisomy 18; Omphalocele, diaphragmatic defect, sternal cleft, pericardial defect, cardiac anomalies / ectopia cordis | Trisomy 18, Pentalogy of Cantrell | Pentalogy of Cantrell
explanation:
Fetal T2-weighted MRI shows a ventral midline defect with herniation of abdominal contents into a sac (omphalocele), together with features of a thoracoabdominal wall defect.
Pentalogy of Cantrell is a rare midline defect due to failure of development of the ventral mesoderm. The classic components are an upper midline abdominal wall defect (omphalocele), a defect of the lower sternum, a deficiency of the anterior diaphragm, a defect of the diaphragmatic pericardium, and intracardiac anomalies, and it may include ectopia cordis.
key_findings:
Supraumbilical omphalocele with extrusion of abdominal organs
Anterior diaphragmatic and pericardial defects with lower sternal cleft
Cardiac anomalies (ASD, VSD, left ventricular diverticulum); ectopia cordis in severe cases
learning_points:
Prenatal diagnosis is possible with ultrasound in the first trimester, and fetal MRI helps to define the extent of the defect and lung volume. Karyotyping is recommended because of the association with trisomy 18.
Prognosis depends mainly on the cardiac anomalies and on the associated chromosomal abnormalities, and is poor when ectopia cordis is present.
differential_diagnosis:
Isolated omphalocele (look for Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome)
Gastroschisis (no sac, defect to the right of the cord)
Body stalk anomaly or limb-body wall complex
OEIS complex
Isolated ectopia cordis

title: Neuroblastoma (orbital metastasis)
question_text:
What is the characteristic signal on T2-weighted image?
This lesion is associated with a syndrome characterised by rapid, involuntary conjugate fast eye movements. What is the syndrome?
correct_answer:
1) Intermediate signal on T2-weighted images
2) Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome | Intermediate T2 signal, Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome | Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome | Neuroblastoma orbital metastasis | Metastatic neuroblastoma
explanation:
Post-contrast MRI shows an enhancing soft tissue mass in the left orbit and adjacent lateral orbital wall/greater wing of the sphenoid, causing proptosis, in a young child. This is the typical appearance of orbital metastasis from neuroblastoma.
Neuroblastoma is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood and arises in the adrenal gland or sympathetic chain. Orbital and skull metastases cause proptosis and periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes). The tumour is highly cellular, so it shows intermediate T2 signal and restricted diffusion.
A paraneoplastic syndrome, opsoclonus-myoclonus ("dancing eyes, dancing feet"), occurs in a minority.
key_findings:
Enhancing orbital or skull-base mass with sphenoid wing involvement
Intermediate T2 signal, restricted diffusion
Look for the primary tumour in the adrenal gland or retroperitoneum (calcified mass), and MIBG-avid metastases
learning_points:
Urinary catecholamine metabolites (VMA and HVA) are raised, and MIBG scintigraphy or PET assesses extent of disease.
Orbital metastasis is a feature of stage 4 (metastatic) disease in children under 5 years, and the bilateral involvement is common.
differential_diagnosis:
Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma
Leukaemic deposit (chloroma)
Ewing sarcoma, lymphoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Orbital cellulitis or subperiosteal abscess
Lymphatic malformation or capillary haemangioma

title: Wolman disease
question_text:
What deficiency causes this condition?
What are the other abdominal findings that may be present?
correct_answer:
1) Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency
2) Hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy | Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, Hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy | Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency | Wolman disease
explanation:
CT of the abdomen in an infant shows enlarged adrenal glands with bilateral punctate or diffuse calcification, together with hepatosplenomegaly and a low-attenuation liver (steatosis).
Wolman disease is the infantile, severe form of lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (LIPA gene, autosomal recessive). Cholesteryl esters and triglycerides accumulate in lysosomes of the liver, spleen, adrenals, gut and bone marrow, leading to vomiting, diarrhoea, malabsorption and failure to thrive within the first weeks or months of life.
key_findings:
Bilateral enlarged adrenal glands that retain their shape and show calcification
Hepatosplenomegaly with low-attenuation liver
Lymphadenopathy
Thickened bowel wall with malabsorption
learning_points:
The disease is fatal in infancy if untreated. Enzyme replacement therapy (sebelipase alfa) and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation have improved survival.
Cholesteryl ester storage disease is the milder, later-onset form of lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, but adrenal calcification is much less common.
differential_diagnosis:
Old neonatal adrenal haemorrhage
Neuroblastoma
Adrenal tuberculosis or other granulomatous infection
Congenital cytomegalovirus infection
Adrenocortical tumour

title: Os trigonum syndrome (posterior ankle impingement)
question_text:
What tendon is usually impinged?
What is the nomenclature of an elongated lateral tubercle of the posterior process of the talus?
correct_answer:
1) Flexor hallucis longus
2) Stieda process | Flexor hallucis longus, Stieda process | FHL, Stieda process | Os trigonum syndrome | Posterior ankle impingement
explanation:
The sagittal fat-suppressed MRI of the ankle shows an os trigonum, an accessory ossicle posterior to the talus, with surrounding marrow and soft tissue oedema and fluid around the flexor hallucis longus tendon.
Posterior ankle impingement occurs with repeated or forced plantarflexion, as in ballet dancers and footballers. The os trigonum (or a prominent Stieda process, which is an elongated lateral tubercle of the posterior talar process) is compressed between the posterior tibial margin and the calcaneus ("nutcracker" mechanism), and the adjacent flexor hallucis longus tendon becomes inflamed.
key_findings:
Os trigonum or elongated Stieda process
Bone marrow oedema at the synchondrosis or posterior talus
Flexor hallucis longus tenosynovitis, posterior capsular thickening and soft tissue oedema
learning_points:
An os trigonum is present in roughly 10 to 25% of people and is usually asymptomatic. Symptoms appear with repeated plantarflexion.
A fracture of the Stieda process is called a Shepherd fracture.
differential_diagnosis:
Shepherd fracture of the lateral tubercle
Flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy without impingement
Achilles tendinopathy or retrocalcaneal bursitis
Posterior malleolar (Volkmann) fracture
Osteochondral lesion of the talus

title: Developmental venous anomaly
question_text:
What is the name of the sign shown?
What is the characteristic finding on angiography?
correct_answer:
1) Medusa head sign (caput medusae)
2) A collection of dilated medullary veins converging into an enlarged transcortical or subependymal collector vein, seen only in the venous phase. | Medusa head sign (caput medusae), Collector vein in venous phase | Medusa head sign | Caput medusae | Developmental venous anomaly | DVA
explanation:
SWI shows a radial array of small linear hypointense veins converging on a larger draining vein in the cerebellum, the Medusa head (caput medusae) appearance of a developmental venous anomaly (DVA).
A DVA is an anatomical variant of venous drainage in which numerous small medullary veins converge on a single large collector vein that drains into a dural sinus or an ependymal vein. The brain tissue between the veins is normal, and the vein is a functioning part of normal drainage.
key_findings:
Radial dilated medullary veins converging on a collector vein (caput medusae)
Angiography: visible only in the venous phase, with normal arterial and capillary phases
No arteriovenous shunting or nidus
learning_points:
DVA is the most common cerebral vascular malformation and is usually an incidental finding. It should not be resected, as this can cause venous infarction.
DVAs are associated with cavernous malformations in a proportion of patients, and the cavernoma (not the DVA) is the usual cause of haemorrhage.
differential_diagnosis:
Arteriovenous malformation (arterial feeders, nidus, early venous drainage)
Cavernous malformation (popcorn lesion with haemosiderin)
Capillary telangiectasia (brush-like enhancement on SWI)
Dural arteriovenous fistula
Sturge-Weber pial angiomatosis

title: Thyroid eye disease (Graves orbitopathy)
question_text:
What is the typical order of extraocular muscle involvement?
What is the aetiology of the 'Coca-Cola bottle sign'?
correct_answer:
1) Inferior > medial > superior > lateral rectus
2) Thyroid orbitopathy: the anterior tendon is typically spared with swelling of the muscle belly. | Inferior > medial > superior > lateral rectus (I'M SLow), Thyroid orbitopathy tendon sparing | IMSLow, Thyroid eye disease | Thyroid eye disease | Graves orbitopathy
explanation:
The coronal T1-weighted MRI shows enlarged extraocular muscle bellies in both orbits with proptosis, typical of thyroid eye disease (Graves orbitopathy).
Inflammation and glycosaminoglycan deposition cause fusiform enlargement of the muscle belly with sparing of the tendinous insertion, and this gives the muscle a "Coca-Cola bottle" shape on axial images.
key_findings:
Bilateral, usually symmetric, fusiform enlargement of the muscle bellies with tendon sparing
Proptosis and increased orbital fat
Crowding of the muscles at the orbital apex with optic nerve compression is the sight-threatening complication
learning_points:
The mnemonic "I'M SLow" gives the order: inferior, medial, superior, lateral rectus.
Active (oedematous) disease is hyperintense on T2/STIR, and chronic disease is fibrotic. Imaging also assesses apical crowding to determine risk to vision, and decompression is the surgical option.
Graves disease is the commonest cause, though patients may be euthyroid or hypothyroid.
differential_diagnosis:
Idiopathic orbital inflammation (pseudotumour): tendon involvement, usually unilateral and painful
IgG4-related disease
Lymphoma or metastasis
Carotid-cavernous fistula (dilated superior ophthalmic vein)
Orbital myositis

title: Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome
question_text:
What part of the duodenum is compressed?
What angle is measured for diagnosis?
correct_answer:
1) D3 (third part of the duodenum)
2) Aorto-mesenteric angle, normally > 25 degrees | Third part of duodenum (D3), Aorto-mesenteric angle | D3, Aortomesenteric angle | SMA syndrome | Superior mesenteric artery syndrome | Wilkie syndrome
explanation:
The sagittal CT shows a markedly narrowed aorto-mesenteric angle, with compression of the third part of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta, and the axial image shows a dilated, fluid-filled stomach and proximal duodenum.
The third part of the duodenum crosses between the aorta and the SMA, cushioned by a retroperitoneal fat pad. Weight loss and loss of this fat pad narrow the aorto-mesenteric angle (normally 25 to 60 degrees) and distance (normally 10 to 28 mm), and obstruct the duodenum, causing postprandial pain and bilious vomiting.
key_findings:
Aorto-mesenteric angle below about 25 degrees (and distance below about 8 mm)
Abrupt cut-off of D3 with dilated stomach and D1-D2
Loss of the retroperitoneal fat plane
learning_points:
The syndrome is also called Wilkie syndrome. Risk factors include rapid weight loss, anorexia nervosa, burns, prolonged bed rest, and scoliosis correction surgery.
Management is conservative (nutrition, positioning), and surgical duodenojejunostomy is for refractory cases.
differential_diagnosis:
Nutcracker syndrome (left renal vein compression)
Annular pancreas or duodenal web
Duodenal or pancreatic head tumour
Intestinal malrotation with Ladd bands
Adhesions

title: Multiple myeloma
question_text:
What are the 4 clinically defining events in this condition?
What is the most common site of involvement?
correct_answer:
1) CRAB: hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, bone disease
2) Vertebrae | CRAB (hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, bone lesions), Vertebrae | CRAB, Spine / Vertebrae | Multiple myeloma
explanation:
The skull radiograph shows multiple well-defined, "punched-out" lytic lesions of varying size scattered through the calvarium, without sclerotic margins, which is the classical appearance of myeloma ("raindrop" or "pepper-pot" skull).
Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma cell malignancy. Osteoclast activation by tumour cells produces purely lytic lesions with little or no new bone formation, so bone scans are often cold. The spine is the most commonly affected site, followed by the skull, ribs, pelvis and proximal long bones.
key_findings:
Multiple punched-out lytic lesions in the skull, spine, pelvis and ribs
Diffuse osteopenia and vertebral compression fractures
Soft tissue masses from plasmacytomas
learning_points:
Whole-body low-dose CT has replaced the skeletal survey, and MRI is used for marrow infiltration and for cord compression. Diagnostic criteria require clonal bone marrow plasma cells or a plasmacytoma with a myeloma-defining event (CRAB, or biomarkers such as 60% or more marrow plasma cells).
A solitary plasmacytoma may precede systemic disease.
differential_diagnosis:
Lytic metastases (kidney, thyroid, breast, lung)
Hyperparathyroidism: brown tumours and salt-and-pepper skull
Normal arachnoid granulations and venous lakes
Langerhans cell histiocytosis (children)
Paget disease (lytic phase)

title: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
question_text:
What are the two types of this pathology?
What parameter is used antenatally for prognosis?
correct_answer:
1) Morgagni and Bochdalek
2) Lung-to-head ratio (LHR) | Bochdalek and Morgagni, Lung-to-head ratio (LHR) | Morgagni and Bochdalek, LHR | Congenital diaphragmatic hernia | CDH
explanation:
The neonatal chest radiograph shows multiple gas-filled loops of bowel in the left hemithorax with shift of the mediastinum to the right, and a relative paucity of bowel gas in the abdomen.
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a defect in the diaphragm allowing abdominal contents to enter the chest. The Bochdalek hernia (posterolateral, mostly on the left, about 85 to 90%) is the commonest type; the Morgagni hernia is anteromedial and retrosternal, usually on the right.
The compressed developing lung results in pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension, which is the cause of morbidity.
key_findings:
Bowel loops in the hemithorax, mediastinal shift to the opposite side
Nasogastric tube coiled in the chest and paucity of abdominal gas
Ipsilateral lung hypoplasia and hyperinflation of the contralateral lung
learning_points:
The observed-to-expected lung-to-head ratio (o/e LHR) and the position of the liver ("liver up") are the main antenatal prognostic indicators, and fetal MRI total lung volume is also used. Severe cases may be considered for fetoscopic endoluminal tracheal occlusion.
Postnatal management starts with stabilisation, ventilation and treatment of pulmonary hypertension, and surgical repair is done later.
differential_diagnosis:
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation
Congenital lobar emphysema
Bronchogenic cyst
Diaphragmatic eventration
Pneumatocele or pneumothorax

title: Pulmonary chondroma
question_text:
How is this lesion differentiated from a hamartoma?
What syndrome can this condition be associated with?
correct_answer:
1) Hamartomas will demonstrate fat; a chondroma contains cartilaginous calcification but no fat.
2) Carney triad: gastric stromal tumours; extra-adrenal paragangliomas; pulmonary chondromas. | Hamartoma contains fat whereas chondroma has no fat, Carney triad | Carney triad | Pulmonary chondroma
explanation:
CT shows a well-circumscribed lobulated nodule in the left lung with coarse, popcorn-type calcification and no macroscopic fat, in keeping with a pulmonary chondroma.
Pulmonary chondromas are rare benign cartilaginous tumours. In Carney triad (young women, usually non-hereditary) they occur together with gastric GIST and extra-adrenal paraganglioma, and the triad may be incomplete.
key_findings:
Smooth, well-defined nodule with chondroid (popcorn) calcification
No fat attenuation (differs from hamartoma)
Look for gastric wall mass and paragangliomas in a young woman
learning_points:
Pulmonary hamartoma is the commonest benign lung tumour and may also show popcorn calcification, but shows fat on CT.
A related dyad, the Carney-Stratakis syndrome (GIST and paraganglioma), is familial and associated with succinate dehydrogenase mutations.
differential_diagnosis:
Pulmonary hamartoma (fat with or without calcification)
Granuloma (dense, central or diffuse calcification)
Carcinoid tumour
Metastasis from chondrosarcoma or osteosarcoma
Calcified lung carcinoma

title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
clinical_info: Asymmetric ascending spastic quadriparesis with dysphonia
question_text:
Name the sign demonstrated in the first image.
What is the pathological basis of this disease?
correct_answer:
1) Motor band sign
2) Loss of upper motor neurons (Betz cells) and anterior horn cells | Motor band sign, Loss of upper motor neurons (Betz cells) and anterior horn cells | Motor band sign | Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis | ALS
explanation:
The susceptibility-weighted/T2*-weighted image shows a thin band of low signal along the precentral gyrus (the motor cortex), the "motor band sign", which is thought to reflect iron deposition and microglial activation in the degenerating motor cortex.
ALS is a neurodegenerative disease with progressive degeneration of both upper motor neurons (corticospinal tract) and lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells and bulbar nuclei), giving spasticity, hyperreflexia, wasting, fasciculations and bulbar signs such as dysphonia.
key_findings:
Motor band sign: hypointense precentral cortex on SWI/T2*
T2/FLAIR hyperintensity along the corticospinal tract (internal capsule, brainstem)
Precentral gyrus atrophy; MRI of the brain and cervical spine mainly serves to exclude mimics
learning_points:
ALS is a clinical diagnosis (El Escorial and Awaji criteria), supported by electromyography. MRI is used to exclude structural mimics such as cervical spondylotic myelopathy.
The motor band sign is not specific, and may also be seen in healthy older people.
differential_diagnosis:
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
Multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating disease
Primary lateral sclerosis, hereditary spastic paraparesis
Multifocal motor neuropathy, Kennedy disease, post-polio syndrome
Syringomyelia or Hirayama disease

title: CLIPPERS
question_text:
What lymphocytes are primarily involved in this pathology?
What is the treatment?
correct_answer:
1) T cells (CD4)
2) Steroids | CD4 T cells, Steroids | T lymphocytes, Corticosteroids | CLIPPERS
explanation:
Contrast-enhanced axial T1-weighted MRI shows multiple small, punctate and curvilinear enhancing foci ("salt-and-pepper" pattern) in the pons and cerebellum, with no significant mass effect.
CLIPPERS (chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids) is an inflammatory CNS disorder with perivascular infiltration of mainly CD4+ T lymphocytes. Patients present with gait ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria and facial paraesthesia or numbness, and improve dramatically with corticosteroids.
key_findings:
Punctate enhancing foci (less than 3 mm) in the pons, extending to the cerebellum, middle cerebral peduncles and sometimes the spinal cord, decreasing in size and number away from the pons
No restricted diffusion or significant mass effect
Marked improvement of enhancement with steroids
learning_points:
CLIPPERS is a diagnosis of exclusion, and brain biopsy is often needed to exclude CNS lymphoma, which can also respond transiently to steroids.
Relapse on steroid withdrawal is common, and a long taper or steroid-sparing agents are used.
differential_diagnosis:
Primary CNS lymphoma or lymphomatoid granulomatosis
Neurosarcoidosis
Vasculitis or Behçet disease
Multiple sclerosis
Erdheim-Chester disease or other histiocytosis

title: Diffuse astrocytoma
question_text:
What characteristic sign is denoted?
What does the above sign indicate?
correct_answer:
1) T2/FLAIR mismatch sign: homogeneous T2 hyperintensity with partial or near-complete FLAIR suppression.
2) High probability of the lesion being IDH-mutant and 1p/19q non-codeleted. | T2-FLAIR mismatch sign, IDH-mutant 1p/19q non-codeleted astrocytoma | T2/FLAIR mismatch sign | IDH-mutant astrocytoma | Diffuse astrocytoma
explanation:
The multiparametric MRI shows a non-enhancing left temporal lobe mass that is homogeneously hyperintense on T2 but relatively suppressed on FLAIR, apart from a thin hyperintense rim. This is the T2/FLAIR mismatch sign.
The T2/FLAIR mismatch sign is highly specific for IDH-mutant astrocytoma (1p/19q non-codeleted), the molecular subtype to which a diffuse astrocytoma belongs. Microcystic change is thought to explain the mismatch, and its sensitivity is low, but the specificity is nearly 100%.
key_findings:
T2-hyperintense mass with relative FLAIR hypointensity and a thin rim
No or minimal enhancement, no restricted diffusion, little mass effect
Temporal lobe location with seizure or syncope as the presenting event
learning_points:
According to the WHO 2021 classification, astrocytoma is IDH-mutant (grades 2 to 4), and oligodendroglioma is IDH-mutant with 1p/19q codeletion (calcification, cortical involvement, and no mismatch sign).
Maximal safe resection is the aim, followed by molecular grading and adjuvant therapy as required.
differential_diagnosis:
Oligodendroglioma (calcified, heterogeneous)
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype
Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour or ganglioglioma
Pilocytic astrocytoma (cyst with enhancing nodule, children)
Limbic encephalitis

title: Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome
clinical_info: Short stature, delayed milestones and low growth hormone
question_text:
Combination of hyperprolactinaemia and hypothyroidism results in what syndrome?
How is this condition different from ectopic posterior pituitary?
correct_answer:
1) Pickardt syndrome
2) Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome also shows a hypoplastic anterior pituitary (with a thin or absent stalk), in addition to the ectopic posterior pituitary. | Pickardt syndrome, Hypoplastic anterior pituitary with thin/absent stalk | Pickardt syndrome | Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome | PSIS
explanation:
The sagittal T1-weighted MRI shows a small anterior pituitary, a thin or non-visualised pituitary stalk, and an ectopic T1-hyperintense posterior pituitary at the median eminence.
Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome (PSIS) comprises a thin or absent pituitary stalk, an ectopic (or absent) posterior pituitary bright spot, and a hypoplastic or aplastic anterior pituitary. Without the stalk, hypothalamic releasing hormones cannot reach the anterior pituitary, causing growth hormone deficiency and later deficiency of other hormones, while the loss of dopamine inhibition may cause hyperprolactinaemia.
key_findings:
Thin, interrupted or absent pituitary stalk
Ectopic posterior pituitary (T1 bright spot at the median eminence)
Hypoplastic anterior pituitary (small, flattened gland)
Thin-section sagittal and coronal T1 are needed
learning_points:
PSIS is associated with perinatal insults (breech delivery, hypoxia) and with gene mutations (HESX1, LHX4, OTX2, SOX3). Midline anomalies and extrapituitary malformations are common.
Pituitary function must be monitored for evolving deficiencies. Neonates can present with hypoglycaemia and prolonged jaundice.
differential_diagnosis:
Isolated growth hormone deficiency with a normal MRI
Septo-optic dysplasia
Craniopharyngioma or Rathke cleft cyst
Langerhans cell histiocytosis or germinoma (thickened stalk)
Hypophysitis

title: Hypertrophic olivary degeneration
question_text:
The enlargement of what anatomic structure results in this appearance?
What is the pathophysiology of this appearance?
correct_answer:
1) Inferior olivary nucleus
2) Trans-synaptic degeneration caused by a brainstem or cerebellar lesion interrupting the triangle of Guillain and Mollaret (the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway), resulting in hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus. | Inferior olivary nucleus, Trans-synaptic degeneration of Guillain-Mollaret triangle | Inferior olivary nucleus, Guillain-Mollaret triangle | Hypertrophic olivary degeneration | HOD
explanation:
Axial T2-weighted MRI of the medulla shows enlarged and T2-hyperintense inferior olivary nucleus, without enhancement, in a patient with palatal myoclonus.
Hypertrophic olivary degeneration is a form of trans-synaptic degeneration that follows a lesion (haemorrhage, infarct, trauma, surgery or tumour) in the Guillain-Mollaret triangle. The triangle connects the dentate nucleus (via the superior cerebellar peduncle) to the contralateral red nucleus, then the central tegmental tract to the ipsilateral inferior olive, and back to the contralateral cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
key_findings:
Enlarged, T2-hyperintense inferior olive on the side of the lesion in the pathway (ipsilateral central tegmental tract or contralateral dentate nucleus)
No contrast enhancement and no restricted diffusion
Evidence of the primary lesion (old haemorrhage, cavernoma, infarct, surgery)
learning_points:
The MRI evolves over time: T2 hyperintensity appears at about 1 month, hypertrophy at about 6 months, and later the hypertrophy resolves while the hyperintensity persists and the olive finally atrophies.
Clinical presentation is typically with palatal myoclonus (palatal tremor), often months after the insult, and sometimes ocular myoclonus or ataxia.
differential_diagnosis:
Medullary infarct or demyelination
Brainstem tumour or metastasis
Brainstem encephalitis
Wernicke encephalopathy or Leigh disease
